content.content:
# K80 model sizing reference

Which model to run on the Tesla K80 testbed, by how much GPU memory you have.

## The hardware

Each K80 board is two GK210 dies, ~11.4 GiB usable each; this host has two boards
(4 dies). Models split across dies by layer, so the practical question is **how many
dies a model needs** — weights plus KV cache and context. Three tiers matter here;
nothing in the current set needs a fourth die.

| Tier | Dies | ~VRAM | Weight budget |
|---|:--:|--:|---|
| Single die | 1 | 11.4 GiB | ≲ 10 GB |
| Two dies | 2 | 22.8 GiB | ~13–20 GB |
| Three dies | 3 | 34.2 GiB | ~24 GB |

The K80 is a for-fun target — even the two- and three-die models are slow. This table
is for coverage and comparison, not production throughput.

## How to read it

One representative model per family per tier — **Model · Size · what it Represents**.
Sizes are download size (Q4). Two comparison axes are kept intact:

- **Generation** — Gemma 3 vs Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5 vs Qwen 3.6 (`⟷` marks the pair).
- **Like-size** — the same nominal size across generations (Gemma 12b↔12b, Qwen
  27b↔27b and 35b↔35b).

Code-path-only models (`qwen3-vl`, `ornith`, `functiongemma`, qwen3-coder) and
redundant footprints are left out — this is a sizing reference, not a code-path
inventory.

## Single die — ~11.4 GiB

| Model | Size | Represents |
|---|--:|---|
| `gemma3:4b` | 3.3 GB | Gemma 3 — small |
| `gemma3:12b` | 8.1 GB | Gemma 3 — 12B `⟷` |
| `gemma4:12b` | 7.6 GB | Gemma 4 — 12B `⟷` · vision + audio |
| `gemma4:e4b` | 9.6 GB | Gemma 4 — small (native vision) |
| `qwen3.5:9b` | 6.6 GB | Qwen 3.5 — small |
| `deepseek-r1:14b` | 9.0 GB | DeepSeek-R1 — largest 1-die |
| `ministral-3:14b` | 9.1 GB | Ministral-3 — largest 1-die |
| `lfm2.5:8b` | 4.8 GB | LFM2.5 — fun |

## Two dies — ~22.8 GiB

| Model | Size | Represents |
|---|--:|---|
| `gemma3:27b` | 17 GB | Gemma 3 — large `⟷` |
| `gemma4:31b` | 20 GB | Gemma 4 — large `⟷` |
| `qwen3.5:27b` | 17 GB | Qwen 3.5 — 27B `⟷` |
| `qwen3.6:27b` | 17 GB | Qwen 3.6 — 27B `⟷` |
| `deepseek-r1:32b` | 20 GB | DeepSeek-R1 — large |
| `gpt-oss:20b` | 13 GB | gpt-oss — fun |

## Three dies — ~34.2 GiB

| Model | Size | Represents |
|---|--:|---|
| `qwen3.5:35b` | 24 GB | Qwen 3.5 — XL `⟷` |
| `qwen3.6:35b` | 24 GB | Qwen 3.6 — XL `⟷` · showcase |

## Notes

- **gemma4 is not one size ladder.** `12b` (vision **and** audio, separate clip-mmproj
  projector) and `e4b` (native vision only) are different capabilities, not
  interchangeable — both are kept at the single-die tier.
- **Qwen 3.6 has no small model** — its smallest is `27b` (two dies). `qwen3.5:9b`
  stands in for "small Qwen".
- **The three-die tier is Qwen-only** — the `35b` (24 GB) pair. No Gemma or DeepSeek
  reaches it; their largest (~20 GB) fits two dies.
- **Sizes are download size, not runtime VRAM.** Actual dies used include KV cache and
  context and can round a model up a tier at long context — see the measured
  `docs/reports/k80-vram-by-family-*.md` snapshots.

content.text:
Both of your ideas lead to one rule. Each model should cover one combination of **code path × number of GPU dies it loads onto**. Testing several sizes per family is useful because the scheduler has to choose 1, 2 or 3 dies. Two models in the same cell test the same thing twice and take twice the disk space.

Here are the 20 models placed on that grid:

```
                            1 die (≤11.4G)         2 dies               3 dies
                            ───────────────        ───────────────      ───────────────
GO ENGINE
 gemma3 (inline vision)     gemma3:4b    3.3G  ┐   gemma3:27b  17.4G    ·
                            gemma3:12b   8.1G  ┘◄ duplicate
 gemma3 (text only)         functiongemma 0.3G     ·                    ·
 gemma4 (inline vision)     gemma4:e4b   9.6G      ·                    gemma4:31b 19.9G
 mistral3                   ministral-3:14b 9.1G   ·                    ·
 gptoss                     ·                      gpt-oss:20b 13.8G    ·
 qwen3vl / qwen3vlmoe       qwen3-vl:8b  6.1G      qwen3-vl:30b 19.6G   ·
 qwen35 dense               qwen3.5:9b   6.6G  ┐   ·                    ·
                            ornith:9b    5.6G  ┘◄ duplicate
 qwen35moe                  ·                      ·                    ornith:35b  21.2G ┐
 qwen35 split projector     ·                      qwen3.6:27b 17.8G    qwen3.6:35b 22.6G ┘◄ duplicate
LLAMA.CPP
 qwen2                      ·                      deepseek-r1:14b 9.0G deepseek-r1:32b 19.9G
 lfm2 / lfm2moe             lfm2.5:8b    5.2G      ·                    ·
                            lfm2.5-thinking 0.7G
 gemma4 split projector     ·                      gemma4:12b   7.6G    ·
```

Die counts are measured at a 4k context where a measurement exists (`docs/reports/k80-vram-by-family-2026-07-10-d83061de.md`). The rest come from what each testcase says it expects.

## Idea 1: covering 1, 2 and 3 dies

The grid shows three pairs where two models test the same path at the same die count:

| Drop | Kept model covering the same cell | Frees |
|---|---|--:|
| `ornith:35b` | `qwen3.6:35b` runs the same qwen35moe code on 3 dies; the extra projector doesn't change text generation | 21.2 GB |
| `gemma3:12b` | `gemma3:4b`, same code on 1 die | 8.1 GB |
| `ornith:9b` | `qwen3.5:9b`, same qwen35 arch on 1 die | 5.6 GB |

That frees **34.9 GB**, taking the runner from **223 GB to 188 GB**, and no cell loses coverage.

Two things I'd keep even though they look like overlaps:
- **Both lfm2 models.** They use different architecture variants, and `lfm2.5-thinking` guards the loader fix from #438. It is also only 0.7 GB.
- **`functiongemma`.** A text-only gemma3 model allocates GPU memory differently from gemma3 with vision, and it costs 0.3 GB.

The trade-off: dropping the two ornith models means nothing regression-tests the ornith tags specifically. Only their code path stays covered.

## Idea 2: disk use keeps growing

A rule for each new model: it keeps a permanent place on the runner only if it fills an **empty cell** in the grid. If its cell is already covered, run it for its own port issue and then remove it. Its testcase can stay in the repo as that issue's acceptance record, marked so it isn't part of the default suite.

The empty cells show where a new model would add real coverage:
- Nothing tests **2 dies on the Go engine with gemma4**.
- Nothing tests **1 die on the qwen35 split-projector path**.

`docs/k80-model-sizing.md` is out of date. It lists deepseek-r1:14b and gemma4:12b as fitting on 1 die, and gemma4:31b and deepseek-r1:32b as fitting on 2. Measured, each of the four needs one more die than that. If this becomes the trim policy, that doc should be updated too.

Should I trim the three models, which means deleting their testcases and updating the sizing doc? Or file it as an issue first?

content.text:
Yes, the idea is still worth it, but it now belongs somewhere else. The code that picks how many dies to use is shared by every model, so each family doesn't need its own ladder of sizes to test it. What changes per architecture is the memory estimate that code works from. And almost every die-count bug so far only appeared at long context, which the models suite never runs.

```
               how a model ends up on N dies
               ─────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. memory estimate          ◄── DIFFERENT per arch/engine │
  │    llama.cpp: llm/memory.go:238 + fs/ggml/ggml.go:553     │
  │    Go engine: measured at load (llm/server.go:736)        │
  │    + num_batch clamp by arch/size (llm/server.go:257)     │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 2. pick fewest dies         ◄── SHARED, one code path     │
  │    assignLayers / findBestFit / greedyFit                 │
  │    llm/server.go:1123-1192                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  past die-count bugs — all in box 1, per arch:
   #72  qwen35     #440 qwen35moe (long ctx)   #453 gptoss   (long ctx)
   #73  llama eng  #451 gemma4 SWA (high ctx)  #452 qwen35 27b (long ctx)
   #352 qwen2      #455 qwen35 9b              gemma4:26b → 4 dies @8k
```

## Why the models suite doesn't test this

- **Every models testcase runs at 4k context.** The size-based clamps at `llm/server.go:257` only take effect above 32k. At 4k, all 20 models take the same branch, so the size-specific code never runs.
- **Most of the long-context bugs (#440, #451, #452, #453) were found by `test-report-sweep` and the fit-map**, which sweep context from 2k up to 192k. That workflow is where scheduling is actually tested, and it covers 8 models.

## What to cover instead

The unit of coverage becomes **one model per memory-estimate branch**, tested in the sweep:

```
branch                         model(s) now              keep
qwen35   BlockCount>=48        qwen3.6:27b               ✔
qwen35   BlockCount<48         qwen3.5:9b, ornith:9b     one of them
qwen35moe                      qwen3.6:35b, ornith:35b   one of them
gptoss                         gpt-oss:20b               ✔
gemma4   (SWA estimate)        e4b, 12b, 31b             ✔ ×3: inline / split projector / 3-die
qwen2    (llama.cpp estimate)  deepseek-r1:14b, 32b      ✔ ×2: 2-die / 3-die
gemma3                         4b, 12b, 27b              4b + 27b; 12b adds nothing
```

That supports the same three drops as before: ornith:9b, ornith:35b and gemma3:12b, freeing about 35 GB. The reason is different, though: they duplicate an existing memory-estimate branch.

This also answers your disk-space point. When a new model is added, the question is whether it brings a new estimate branch (new architecture, new engine path, or new size split in the code). If it doesn't, test it once for its port issue and then remove it from the runner.

You're right. I understated that last time. The step that places layers on dies is shared, but what it's given is hardcoded per model family in five places:

```
                              ┌─────────────── HARDCODED BY FAMILY ───────────────┐
request ─► server/sched.go:418  numParallel=1 for mllama, qwen3vl, qwen3vlmoe
             │
             ▼
           llm/memory.go:30     num_batch table: deepseek2=2048, qwen2/gemma3/
             │                  mistral3/gptoss…=512, anything unlisted → 512
             ▼
           llm/server.go:257    num_batch clamp by context (only above 32k):
             │                    qwen35moe · qwen35 ≥48 blocks · qwen35 <48 · gptoss
             ▼
           fs/ggml/ggml.go:889  flash-attention allow/deny by family
             │                              └──────────────────────────────────────┘
             ▼
     ┌───────┴────────────────────────────────┐
     │ LLAMA.CPP engine                       │ GO engine
     │ llm/server.go:584                      │ llm/server.go:781
     │ estimateGPULayers → GraphSize()        │ runner does a "Fit" pass and
     │ fs/ggml/ggml.go:616 switch per family: │ reports its real allocation
     │   llama · gemma* · qwen2 · deepseek2   │ (resp.Memory) ─ no family formula
     │   gptoss · … · default                 │
     │ × graphSafetyMultiplier 2.5 (:402)     │
     └───────┬────────────────────────────────┘
             ▼
     createLayout / findBestFit / greedyFit   ◄── shared: fewest dies that fit
     llm/server.go:1123-1192
```

## What this means for the test list

- **llama.cpp models** (deepseek-r1 → qwen2, lfm2.5 → lfm2/lfm2moe, gemma4:12b): die count depends on the per-family `GraphSize()` formula × 2.5. lfm2 isn't in that switch, so it gets the default formula. Each family here needs its own coverage, as you remembered.
- **Go engine models** (gemma3, gemma4 e4b/31b, qwen35, qwen3vl, mistral3, gptoss): die count comes from memory the runner actually allocated, not a formula. Family only matters through the batch table, the clamps and flash attention. Within a family, size matters only where the code checks it, and the only such check is qwen35 at `BlockCount() >= 48`.
- **Model size matters only when the model is near a die boundary.** Your per-family ladder of sizes still earns its place where the estimate is a formula: deepseek-r1:14b and 32b both stay. It adds nothing where the runner measures real memory and nothing branches on size. So the three drops still hold: gemma3:12b, ornith:9b and ornith:35b.

The clamps at `:257` only take effect above 32k, and the models suite runs at 4k. At 4k, the family rules that actually apply are the batch table, flash attention and `GraphSize()`.

content.content:
For Docker Compose and the full configuration, see [docker/README.md](docker/README.md).

## Tested Models

![Small models run at full precision or Q8, medium at Q4_K_M, large at Q4_0 or multi-GPU](docs/images/readme/model-sizing.png)

A K80 has **12 GB VRAM per GPU** (24 GB for a dual-GPU board). Size quantization to fit:

| Model size    | Quantization         |
|---------------|----------------------|
| Small (1–4B)  | Full precision or Q8 |
| Medium (7–8B) | Q4_K_M               |
| Large (13B+)  | Q4_0 or multi-GPU    |

Verified on K80: `gemma3:4b`, `gemma3:27b`, `gemma4:e4b`, `gemma4:26b`, `qwen3.5:9b`,
`qwen3.5:27b`, `gpt-oss:20b`, `deepseek-r1:7b`, `ministral-3`, `functiongemma`.

## How It's Built

Ollama37 is split into two Docker images so the thing you run stays small:

![Source compiles in a ~15 GB builder image into a ~1 GB runtime image, published to Docker Hub](docs/images/readme/build-pipeline.png)

- **`ollama37-builder` (~15 GB)** — the build environment only: CUDA 11.4 toolkit, GCC 10
  and CMake 4 (compiled from source, ~90 min the first time), and Go. It is never shipped.
- **`ollama37` (~1 GB)** — a multi-stage build. The code is compiled *inside* the builder
  with the `CUDA 11 K80` preset (native CUBIN for `sm_37`–`sm_86`, the 470 datacenter sweep), then only the
  artifacts — the `ollama` binary, the GGML/CUDA libraries, the bundled CUDA runtime libs
  (cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cudart), and the GCC 10 runtime libs — are copied onto a slim
  `rockylinux:8-minimal` base. This is the image published to Docker Hub.

To build it yourself:
481	OPEN	Support muse-glimmer (Meta 30B, perception encoder, vision + tools + thinking) on the K80

For Docker Compose and the full configuration, see [docker/README.md](docker/README.md).

## Tested Models

![Small models run at full precision or Q8, medium at Q4_K_M, large at Q4_0 or multi-GPU](docs/images/readme/model-sizing.png)

A K80 has **12 GB VRAM per GPU** (24 GB for a dual-GPU board). Size quantization to fit:

| Model size    | Quantization         |
|---------------|----------------------|
| Small (1–4B)  | Full precision or Q8 |
| Medium (7–8B) | Q4_K_M               |
| Large (13B+)  | Q4_0 or multi-GPU    |

Verified on K80: `gemma3:4b`, `gemma3:27b`, `gemma4:e4b`, `gemma4:26b`, `qwen3.5:9b`,
`qwen3.5:27b`, `gpt-oss:20b`, `deepseek-r1:7b`, `ministral-3`, `functiongemma`.

## How It's Built

Ollama37 is split into two Docker images so the thing you run stays small:

![Source compiles in a ~15 GB builder image into a ~1 GB runtime image, published to Docker Hub](docs/images/readme/build-pipeline.png)

- **`ollama37-builder` (~15 GB)** — the build environment only: CUDA 11.4 toolkit, GCC 10
  and CMake 4 (compiled from source, ~90 min the first time), and Go. It is never shipped.
- **`ollama37` (~1 GB)** — a multi-stage build. The code is compiled *inside* the builder
  with the `CUDA 11 K80` preset (native CUBIN for `sm_37`–`sm_86`, the 470 datacenter sweep), then only the
  artifacts — the `ollama` binary, the GGML/CUDA libraries, the bundled CUDA runtime libs
  (cuBLAS, cuBLASLt, cudart), and the GCC 10 runtime libs — are copied onto a slim
  `rockylinux:8-minimal` base. This is the image published to Docker Hub.

Seen this way, the models suite covers less than the family list suggests:
- **It mostly tests text only.** Only `TC-MODELS-016` (gemma4:12b) sends an image. Six families support images, and five of them never get an image in the models suite.
- **It checks tool calls only for functiongemma** (`TC-MODELS-005`). Tool calls for the other families are checked in `test-mcp.yml`, which isn't part of this suite.

content.text:
Choose **by architecture**, and use popularity only to decide which tag stands in for each one.

A regression test is there to catch the code breaking, and the code breaks per architecture and engine path, not per brand. For example:
- ornith:9b and qwen3.5:9b run the same code at `qwen35/model.go`. If that code breaks, both fail together. If it works, both pass. Testing both adds no information.
- deepseek-r1 is popular, but it's only interesting here because it's the qwen2 path on llama.cpp.

If you choose by popularity, you end up testing the same path many times over and skipping rare paths. lfm2 and the gemma4 separate-projector path are exactly where the fork carries its own patches, so they're the most likely to break.

Popularity still helps in two places:
1. **Picking the representative tag within an architecture.** Users run it, so a break there hurts the most people.
2. **Deciding how deep to go.** Popular families get the capability checks (image, tool calls, thinking). Rare paths get a basic check that the model loads and answers.

```
Suite rule: one row per code path (arch × engine × projector)
            tag = most-used model on that path, smallest that still hits the path

  path                                  representative         extra depth (popular)
  ──────────────────────────────────── ─────────────────────── ─────────────────────
  Go  gemma3  inline vision             gemma3:4b              + image
  Go  gemma4  inline vision+audio       gemma4:e4b             + image, tools
  Go  mistral3                          ministral-3:14b
  Go  gptoss                            gpt-oss:20b            + tools
  Go  qwen3vl                           qwen3-vl:8b            + image
  Go  qwen35  dense, inline vision      qwen3.5:9b             + image, tools
  Go  qwen35  split projector           qwen3.6:27b            + image, tools
  Go  qwen35moe                         qwen3.6:35b
  cpp qwen2                             deepseek-r1:14b
  cpp lfm2 / lfm2moe                    lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b   (+ lfm2.5:8b for moe)
  cpp gemma4  split projector           gemma4:12b             + image, audio
  ──────────────────────────────────── ─────────────────────── ─────────────────────
  11–12 models instead of 20

Everything else (ornith ×2, gemma3:12b/27b, functiongemma, qwen3-vl:30b,
deepseek-r1:32b, gemma4:31b) → port-acceptance only: testcase kept, not in the
default suite, model removed from the runner after its issue closes.
Die-count scheduling → stays in test-report-sweep (it runs long context; the suite doesn't).
```

This also sets the rule for a new model: if it adds a new path, it gets a new row. If it doesn't, it's tested once for its port issue and then leaves the runner.

Two choices in this plan could reasonably go the other way:
- **gemma3:27b and qwen3-vl:30b** could stay if you want the models suite to also cover loading onto 2 dies. I've left that to the sweep.
- **Representative tags here are picked on size and fit, not real pull counts.** I haven't fetched pull counts, since you stopped that request. I can fetch them if you want the "most popular" choice to be real.

For gemma3, the code has three paths, and each path needs one tag. All five sizes run on the Go engine through `model/models/gemma3/`.

```
gemma3  (Go engine, model/models/gemma3/)
│
├─ A. no vision tower  →  ErrNoVisionModel on images          model.go:90
│     ├─ 270m   0.29 GB   0 v.* tensors
│     └─ 1b     0.82 GB   0 v.* tensors
│
├─ B. vision tower, normal query scale                        model_vision.go
│     │  q × 1/√attnKeyLen                                    model_text.go:95
│     ├─ 4b     3.3 GB
│     └─ 12b    8.1 GB
│
└─ C. vision tower, LARGE-MODEL query scale                   model_text.go:63
      │  only when block_count == 62                          model_text.go:34
      │  q × 1/√(hiddenSize/numHeads)                         model_text.go:93
      └─ 27b    17.4 GB
```

I checked `270m` and `1b` in the registry. Neither has a separate projector file, and neither contains any image tensors.

**Pull list for gemma3**

| Path | Pull | Skip | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. text only | `gemma3:270m` | 1b | same code; 270m is the smallest |
| B. vision | `gemma3:4b` | 12b | same code; 4b is also the `TC-INFERENCE` default |
| C. 27b query scale | `gemma3:27b` | none | this code only runs for 27b, so no smaller model can replace it |

Pulling those three costs **21.0 GB**. The current set (4b, 12b, 27b) costs 28.8 GB and never exercises path A.

One thing depends on a later family. `functiongemma:270m` is also the gemma3 architecture with no image tensors, so it runs path A too. If we keep functiongemma for its own renderer and parser, it already covers A and `gemma3:270m` can be dropped, which brings gemma3 down to **4b + 27b**. I'd settle that when we reach functiongemma.

content.text:
The registry has repackaged gemma4:26b, and that tag no longer loads. That's why #484 is still open. The other four tags cover three separate code paths.

```
gemma4
│
├─ GO ENGINE  (no projector file → model/models/gemma4/)
│  │
│  ├─ A. per-layer embeddings + shared KV + vision + audio
│  │     PerLayerProjector branch          model_text.go:186 region
│  │     kvDonorMap (shared_kv_layers)     model_text.go:127 / :218 region
│  │     audio encoder                     model.go:166, model_audio.go
│  │     ├─ e2b    7.2 GB   35 blocks   v=656 a=744
│  │     └─ e4b    9.6 GB   42 blocks   v=656 a=744
│  │
│  └─ B. plain dense + vision, no PLE / no shared KV / no audio
│        └─ 31b   19.9 GB   60 blocks   v=351 a=0
│
└─ LLAMA.CPP  (projector file → "split vision models aren't supported", llm/server.go:167)
   │  llm_build_gemma4_iswa  llama-model.cpp:11173  +  clip.cpp gemma4uv/gemma4ua
   │
   ├─ C. dense
   │     └─ 12b    7.6 GB   48 blocks   projector
   │
   └─ D. MoE + projector + draft layer                ✗ BROKEN (#484, open)
         └─ 26b   18.6 GB   30 blocks   ffn_*_exps ×90
               llm_build_gemma4_iswa has no expert code →
               "wrong number of tensors; expected 658, got 418"
               (draft layer: no case in server/images.go:358 — ignored)
```

**Pull list for gemma4**

| Path | Pull | Skip | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. PLE + shared KV + audio | `gemma4:e2b` | e4b | same code; saves 2.4 GB |
| B. dense on Go engine | `gemma4:31b` | none | the only tag that runs the Go gemma4 path without PLE or shared KV |
| C. llama.cpp dense, separate projector | `gemma4:12b` | none | the only tag on the fork's llama.cpp gemma4 port |
| D. MoE + separate projector | `gemma4:26b` | none | broken now; this becomes the regression test for the #484 fix |

Pulling all four costs **53.3 GB**. Dropping path B brings it to **33.4 GB**, but then the Go engine's no-PLE branch goes untested.

## About #484

The fork's README lists gemma4:26b as "Verified on K80", and the July report measured it running. The registry has since added a separate projector file and a draft model to that tag. So it now falls back to llama.cpp, whose gemma4 builder can't handle mixture-of-experts. There are two ways to fix it:
1. Let gemma4 with a separate projector stay on the Go engine, the same way `qwen35` does at `llm/server.go:163`. The Go package already has the MoE code (`TextMoEBlock`, `model_text.go:342`).
2. Add mixture-of-experts support to the llama.cpp gemma4 builder.

Option 1 matches what #479 just did for qwen35, and it might also let 12b move off llama.cpp.

Two things I haven't checked: whether e2b and e4b hit any other size-based branch in the code, and what the draft layer is for.

Next family: qwen3.5, qwen3.6, qwen3.8 and ornith (the qwen35 architecture)?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Pull the per-arch regression models, skipping any already present.
# Usage: pull-models.sh [model ...]   (defaults to the list below)
set -u

MODELS=("$@")
[ ${#MODELS[@]} -eq 0 ] && MODELS=(
  # gemma3 — A text-only, B vision, C 27b query scale
  gemma3:270m
  gemma3:4b
  gemma3:27b
  # gemma4 — A PLE+shared KV+audio, B Go dense, C llama.cpp split, D MoE split (#484)
  gemma4:e2b
  gemma4:31b
  gemma4:12b
  gemma4:26b
)

have=$(ollama list | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}')
failed=()
for m in "${MODELS[@]}"; do
  if grep -qxF "$m" <<<"$have"; then
    echo "[skip] $m already present"
    continue
  fi
  echo "[pull] $m  $(date '+%F %T')"
  if ollama pull "$m" >/dev/null; then
    echo "[ok]   $m  $(date '+%F %T')"
  else
    echo "[FAIL] $m"
    failed+=("$m")
  fi
done

echo "done. failed: ${failed[*]:-none}"
[ ${#failed[@]} -eq 0 ]

commit 0c5eb3bd8491f5c9ee93693117aeed13395fadc8
Author: Shang Chieh Tseng <[REDACTED-email]>
Date:   Sat Sep 19 21:24:16 2026 +0800

    feat(#479): run qwen3.8 text, tools and thinking on the K80
    
    The registry's qwen3.8:27b is a llama.cpp-format qwen35 GGUF: a trailing MTP
    (nextn) block counted in block_count, 4-entry rope.dimension_sections, and the
    vision tower in a separate qwen3vl_merger projector. The fork routed it to the
    vendored llama.cpp because of the projector, which rejects the rope sections
    ("expected 3, got 4") and has no qwen3vl_merger, so the model never loaded.
    
    Upstream has no engine code to port: it dropped the Go engine for
    llama-server in May 2026. The fork's Go qwen35 model already reads this
    layout's ssm_dt.bias and v-head order and is proven on the K80 with
    qwen3.5/3.6, so text goes there instead:
    
    - qwen35: build block_count - nextn_predict_layers layers. The backend still
      loads the MTP block; the model no longer mistakes it for a DeltaNet layer.
    - llm/server: run qwen35/qwen35moe with a split projector text-only on the
      Ollama engine instead of falling back to a runner that cannot load it.
      Vision is the next step; until then images are ignored (known gap).
    - Renderer: port upstream's qwen3.8 variant of Qwen35Renderer (55127975,
      0f25c31b, 87abaa01, b8a62724). Dropped upstream's no-user-query check:
      chatPrompt renders trailing suffixes while fitting the context window and
      fails on the first render error, so a tool-loop turn [assistant(tool_calls),
      tool] must render or every second tool turn 400s.
    - Parser: qwen3.8 ships parser "qwen3.5", which the fork maps to the JSON-tool
      Qwen3VLParser, but the renderer prompts for XML tool calls. Resolve it to a
      "qwen3.8" Qwen35Parser at model load. That parser honours per-request
      think:false through an optional SetThinkValue hook; ornith keeps forcing
      thinking because its renderer ignores think.
    - Parser: port upstream's leading-whitespace trim after <think> (55127975).
    
    Tests: upstream's qwen38 renderer/parser tests, minus the cases the fork
    cannot reach (MLX tokenizer; xhigh/max think strings the API rejects; the
    Qwen3CoderParser done-flush the fork lacks), plus a tool-loop suffix test.
    
    Verified on the local 4x K80 (sm_37, CUDA 11.4): coherent 194-token answer at
    2.74 tok/s over two dies, thinking routed to the thinking channel,
    think:false answers in content, no-arg tool call and the tool-result turn
    both succeed.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <[REDACTED-email]>

content.text:
For this family, qwen3.8:27b and qwen3.6:35b cover every path that 3.6 and 3.8 have. qwen3.6:27b runs the same model code as 3.8, and 3.6:35b already covers its renderer.

Your working tree is now on `ci-models-override` (`c58d582f`), which doesn't include the #479 commits. The trace below is from `issue-479-qwen38-vision` (`8f4e9895`). On main, the tags with a separate projector file behave differently; see the end.

```
qwen35 family  (Go engine, model/models/qwen35/)          renderer / parser (from registry config)
│
├─ llama.cpp-format GGUF: MTP nextn block + split qwen3vl_merger projector
│  │  layers = block_count − nextn_predict_layers      qwen35/model.go:555
│  │  projector → ml/backend/ggml/projector.go → qwen3vl vision
│  │  stays on Go because arch is qwen35/moe            llm/server.go:163
│  │
│  ├─ dense (64+1 blocks, ssm)
│  │   ├─ qwen3.8:27b   17.7 GB  ─ renderer qwen3.8 → parser rewritten to qwen3.8 (server/images.go:353)
│  │   │                           = Qwen35Renderer (XML tools) + Qwen35Parser
│  │   └─ qwen3.6:27b   17.8 GB  ─ renderer qwen3.5 / parser qwen3.5
│  │                               = Qwen3VLRenderer + Qwen3VLParser (JSON tools)
│  └─ MoE (40+1 blocks, 123 exps)
│      └─ qwen3.6:35b   22.6 GB  ─ renderer qwen3.5 / parser qwen3.5
│
└─ Ollama-format GGUF: vision inline, no MTP block
   └─ dense (32 blocks)
       └─ qwen3.5:9b     6.6 GB  ─ renderer qwen3.5 / parser qwen3.5
                                   inline v.* → qwen35/model.go:688
```

**Pull list for the qwen35 family**

| Path | Pull | Skip | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| dense + separate projector + **qwen3.8 renderer/parser** | `qwen3.8:27b` ✔ already have | qwen3.6:27b | same model code as 3.8; its renderer is covered by 3.6:35b |
| MoE + separate projector + **qwen3.5 renderer/parser** | `qwen3.6:35b` | none | the only qwen35moe tag; also covers the Qwen3VL renderer/parser path |
| Ollama-format GGUF, image data in the model file | `qwen3.5:9b`? | none | **your call**, see below |

That's **22.6 GB** to pull, or 29.2 GB with qwen3.5:9b.

`qwen3.5:9b` is from an older generation, but it's the only qwen35 tag packaged as an Ollama-format file with the image data inside it. Every 3.6 and 3.8 tag is llama.cpp-format with a separate projector file. Dropping it leaves that loader branch (`qwen35/model.go:688`) untested. It costs 6.6 GB. I'd keep it, but it's your call.

## On main, the current registry tags likely break

`llm/server.go:163`, which keeps qwen35 on the Go engine even when it has a projector file, exists only on the #479 branch. On main, any qwen35 tag with a projector falls back to the bundled llama.cpp. The #479 commit message says that path fails on 3.8's format ("expected 3, got 4" rope sections, and no qwen3vl_merger).

The registry's qwen3.6:27b and 35b now have the same format as 3.8: a separate projector file and an extra MTP block. So on main they probably fail the same way gemma4:26b does in #484. The CI host likely still runs older copies of those tags. I haven't run this, so it's inferred from the code and the commit message.

content.text:
**qwen3-vl vs qwen3.6.** They share the same vision code but have different text models. Every qwen3-vl text layer is a standard attention layer with a KV cache. qwen3.6 mixes DeltaNet recurrent layers with a full-attention layer every few blocks.

```
                         qwen3-vl (qwen3vl / qwen3vlmoe)        qwen3.6 (qwen35 / qwen35moe)
                         ─────────────────────────────────      ─────────────────────────────────
Go package               model/models/qwen3vl/                  model/models/qwen35/
Text layers              all full attention (GQA)               Gated DeltaNet (recurrent) +
                         model_text.go:44 TextAttention         full attention every N layers
                                                                inferRecurrentLayers  model.go:497
Cache                    plain KV cache                         HybridCache (KV + recurrent state)
MoE                      sparse{} ffn_*_exps  model_text.go:79  sparse{}  model.go:101
Vision tower             qwen3vl.VisionModel + deepstack  ◄──── SAME CODE: qwen35/model.go:238
                                                                imports qwen3vl.VisionModel
How vision ships         inside the model file (v.* inline)     separate qwen3vl_merger projector
                                                                + MTP block (llama.cpp format)
Renderer / parser        qwen3-vl-thinking                      qwen3.5
                         └─► Qwen3VLRenderer{isThinking:true} ◄─ SAME (renderer.go:59)
Scheduler rules          numParallel=1  server/sched.go:418     num_batch clamps llm/server.go:258-262
                                                                flash attention denied fs/ggml/ggml.go:889
```

This affects your 3.6 decision. The qwen3.5 renderer that 3.6 uses is the same object as qwen3-vl's (`Qwen3VLRenderer{isThinking:true}`), so qwen3-vl already covers it. Once 3.8 is in CI, 3.6:35b's only unique coverage is qwen35moe.

**The qwen3-vl tags from the registry**

```
qwen3vl (dense)       2b    1.9 GB  28 blocks  output tied to token_embd (no output.weight)
                      4b    3.3 GB  36 blocks  tied
                      8b    6.1 GB  36 blocks  separate output.weight
                      32b  20.9 GB  64 blocks  separate output
qwen3vlmoe (MoE)      30b  19.6 GB  48 blocks  144 exps
                      235b 143.3 GB 94 blocks  282 exps   ✗ exceeds 4×K80 (45.8 GB pooled)
```

All six carry the image data in the model file and use the `qwen3-vl-thinking` renderer and parser. The only thing that varies by size is whether the output weights are tied to the input embeddings (`gguf:"output,alt:token_embd"`, `model_text.go:155`). That's generic loader code, and gemma3 exercises the tied case too.

**Pull list for qwen3-vl**

| Path | Pull | Skip | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3vl dense | `qwen3-vl:2b` | 4b, 8b, 32b | same code; 2b is the smallest (1.9 GB vs 8b's 6.1 GB) |
| qwen3vlmoe | `qwen3-vl:30b` | 235b | the only MoE tag that fits on the K80 |

That's **21.5 GB**. The suite currently tests 8b; switching to 2b saves 4.2 GB and loses no code path.

Barely. Ornith runs the same qwen35 model code and reuses qwen3.8's renderer and parser. The only thing it adds is packaging: its qwen35moe file is Ollama-format, with no MTP block and no projector.

```
                     ornith:9b          qwen3.5:9b         ornith:35b         qwen3.6:35b
                     ────────────       ────────────       ────────────       ────────────
arch                 qwen35 dense       qwen35 dense       qwen35moe          qwen35moe
blocks               32                 32                 40 (120 exps)      40+1 MTP (123 exps)
GGUF format          Ollama             Ollama             Ollama             llama.cpp
vision               none               inline v.*         none               split projector
MTP / nextn          no                 no                 no                 yes
Go model code        qwen35/  ─────────── same ──────────  qwen35/  ────────── same
renderer             OrnithRenderer     Qwen3VLRenderer    OrnithRenderer     Qwen3VLRenderer
```

```
mistral3  (Go engine, model/models/mistral3/)   parser "ministral"  → not in fork → nil

│                                               (server/images.go:112)

│             vision.block_count=24 inline   → model_vision.go
│
├─ 3b    3.0 GB  26 blocks  output tied to token_embd   freq_base 1e6
├─ 8b    6.0 GB  34 blocks  separate output             freq_base 1e6
└─ 14b   9.1 GB  40 blocks  separate output             freq_base 1e9   ← value only, same code
```

**Pull list for ministral-3**

| Path | Pull | Skip | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| mistral3 (YaRN + inline vision) | `ministral-3:3b` | 8b, 14b | same code and branches; saves 6.1 GB compared with the 14b in the suite now |

The 3b is also the tag behind the earlier ministral-3 bugs: #63 (the vision memory reservation) and the traces under `docs/traces/ministral3-*`. So it has a track record of catching problems.

One side finding: the registry sets ministral-3's parser to `"ministral"`, but the fork has no parser by that name (`parsers.go:72` returns nil). Tool calls fall back to the template-based path. That doesn't change the pull list.

Should I queue `ministral-3:3b`? After that come the llama.cpp families: deepseek-r1 (qwen2) and lfm2.5.

```

  model_text.go   YaRN rope branch (:31), original-ctx branch (:78)
  model_vision.go Pixtral-style vision tower
  imageproc.go    its own image preprocessing
  fs/ggml/ggml.go:844  its own vision graph-size case
```

Dropping the family would leave all of that untested, including the vision-memory estimate that caused #63. The fork has put real work into this path: #63, and three traces in `docs/traces/` (`ministral3-compute-buffer`, `-garbage-output`, `-memory-usage`).

The only reason to drop it would be deciding the fork no longer supports mistral3. That's a support decision, not a test-trimming one. If you want that, the README and the sizing doc would need updating too.

content.text:
I agree: drop functiongemma. On the model side it adds nothing now. Its only code path is text-only gemma3, which `gemma3:270m` covers, and that's already pulled.

What goes untested: the fork ported `model/renderers/functiongemma.go` and `model/parsers/functiongemma.go`, and neither has a unit test. `TC-MODELS-005` is the only thing that runs them. Once it's gone, a break there would only show up when a user reports it. I think that's acceptable: it's a 270m niche model, and both files are copies of upstream code that rarely change. A GPU slot in CI is the wrong price to pay to protect them. If you want protection back later, a CPU-only `functiongemma_test.go` is cheap and runs without a GPU.

TC-005 is also the only models test that sends `tools`. Tool calls are still checked in `test-mcp.yml`, so that coverage doesn't disappear.

Both lfm2 tags are queued after deepseek-r1:1.5b. The decision log now has lfm2 as keep-as-is, functiongemma as delete TC-005, and gemma3:270m as add.

## Next: the gaps

These are three code paths the fork ships with no test at all:

| Gap | Code | Candidate |
|---|---|---|
| **qwen3 / qwen3moe** | Go `model/models/qwen3/` + qwen3coder renderer/parser | deepseek-r1:8b (qwen3 dense), qwen3 or qwen3-coder tags |
| **llama** | llama.cpp `llm_build_llama`, GraphSize case "llama" | a small llama3.x tag |
| **gemma3n** | Go `model/models/gemma3n/` | gemma3n e2b/e4b |

Which one first? I'd start with qwen3, since it has the most fork-specific code: its own renderer and parser, plus the thinking special case at `server/images.go:176`.

content.content:
# CI-only override: serve models from the CI host's model store.
#
# The only difference from docker-compose.yml is where models come from. The
# testbed's store is an NFS share mounted on the host, bind-mounted here over
# /root/.ollama/models; everything else (image, port, keys in the ollama-data
# volume) is the public compose file, so CI keeps exercising what users run.
#
# The CI host enables it through the runner's .env, not the workflows:
#   COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.ci.yml
#   OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR=/path/to/models
# Every `docker compose` call runs from docker/, so the relative paths resolve.
#
# Models are pulled from the host as the share's owner; the container only
# reads them, so NFS root squashing never applies.
services:
  ollama:
    volumes:
      - ${OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR:?OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR must be set on the CI host}:/root/.ollama/models
The replacement CI host keeps its models on an NFS share (727G free) instead
of the root disk (148G), which cannot hold the models suite. CI and public
users share docker/docker-compose.yml, and the models path is the only thing
that has to differ, so it goes in a separate override rather than an edit
users would inherit.

docker-compose.ci.yml bind-mounts ${OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR} over
/root/.ollama/models; image, port and the ollama-data volume (keys, history)
stay the public file's, so CI still exercises what users run. The CI host
opts in through the runner's .env (COMPOSE_FILE + OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR), so no
workflow or testcase changes: every compose call runs from docker/, and the
two explicit `-f docker-compose.yml` calls only run ps/logs, which the
override does not affect. A missing OLLAMA37_MODELS_DIR fails loudly.

Models are pulled on the host as the share's owner and only read in the
container, so NFS root squashing never applies and the export is untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <[REDACTED-email]>

branch 'ci-models-trim-by-arch' set up to track 'origin/main'.
id: TC-MODELS-011
name: qwen3-vl:8b Inference
suite: models
priority: 4
timeout: 900000
dependencies: []
issue: 55
intent:
  user_story: |
    Validate qwen3-vl:8b runs on K80 compute 3.7 (single GPU)

steps:
  - name: Test inference
    command: |
      curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/generate \
        -d '{"model":"qwen3-vl:8b","prompt":"What is 2+2? Answer briefly.","stream":false,"options":{"num_predict":200}}' \
        | head -c 2000
    expectPatterns:
      - "response"
    rejectPatterns:
      - "CUBLAS_STATUS"
      - "CUDA error"

  - name: Check GPU memory
    command: docker exec ollama37 nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,used_memory --format=csv
    expectPatterns:
      - "[0-9]+ MiB"

  - name: Check GPU count
    command: |
      output=$(docker exec ollama37 nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,used_memory --format=csv,noheader)
      echo "$output"
      active=$(echo "$output" | grep -c 'MiB')
      total=$(echo "$output" | grep -oP '[0-9]+(?= MiB)' | paste -sd+ | bc)
      echo "Active GPUs: $active, Total VRAM: ${total} MiB"
      if [ "$active" -le 1 ]; then
        echo "GPU_COUNT_OK"
      elif [ "$total" -le $(( (active - 1) * 11441 )) ]; then
        echo "GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED: total ${total} MiB fits in $((active - 1)) GPUs but using $active"
      else
        echo "GPU_COUNT_OK"
      fi
    expectPatterns:
      - "GPU_COUNT_OK"
    rejectPatterns:
      - "GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED"

  - name: Unload model
    command: |
      curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/generate \
        -d '{"model":"qwen3-vl:8b","keep_alive":0}'
      echo "Model unloaded"
    expectPatterns:
      - "Model unloaded"

criteria: |
  Validate qwen3-vl:8b (~5GB VRAM, single GPU) runs on K80 (compute 3.7).
  Vision-capable model tested with text-only inference.
  Prerequisite: Model must be pre-pulled before running this test.

  Expected:
  - API returns JSON with "response" field containing coherent text
  - GPU memory is allocated (visible in nvidia-smi)
  - GPU count: model must not use more GPUs than needed. Each K80 GPU has 11441 MiB.
    If total VRAM fits in (active_gpus - 1) GPUs, the model is wasting GPUs.
  - No CUDA/CUBLAS errors in output
  - Model unloads successfully

  Acceptable warnings (NOT errors):

content.content:
## Description
The models-suite "Check GPU count" step counts every GPU on which the runner PID holds *any* memory (`nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps`). When the rare #138 "ghost" allocation (a CUDA primary context, sub-100 MiB) lands on an otherwise layerless die, the step sees N+1 GPUs and reports `GPU_COUNT_EXCEEDED` — failing an otherwise-correct run.

Observed on TC-MODELS-015 (qwen3.6:35b): one run saw **4** GPUs (model layers on 3 + a ghost sliver on a 4th) → failure; the immediate re-run saw the expected **3** → pass. The model produces correct output either way.

## Expected Behavior
The GPU-count check should not fail a run for a sub-~100 MiB ghost allocation. It should distinguish:
- real over-spread (model layers across more dies than needed — GBs per die), from
- a tiny ghost context that merely woke an idle die.

## Proposed Fix
Count a GPU as "used" only when the PID holds more than a small threshold there (e.g. `> 256 MiB`), filtering ghosts. The check is currently inlined per-YAML, so the fix touches each TC-MODELS GPU-count step (or a shared helper).

## Notes
- Root cause of the ghost itself is #138 (CUDA primary context on a layerless GPU). This issue is only about making the **test** robust to it, not fixing the ghost.
- The #184 `/api/metrics` work added a `ghost` flag that identifies exactly this case.

Related to #138

content.text:
The check confirms it:

- **The 5 retargeted cases: steps identical.** Only the model name changed. Same prompt, same `num_predict: 200`, same expect and reject patterns, same GPU-memory, GPU-count and unload steps. No `think` flag added to any of them.
- **TC-023 and TC-024: identical to the template**, no flow change.
- **TC-022 (deepseek-r1:8b) is the one exception.** I added `"think":false` to its inference request, plus a note saying why. Without it, the model spends all 200 tokens in the thinking span and `response` comes back empty, so the case would pass without the model ever answering.

That isn't a new pattern in the suite. TC-016 (gemma4:12b), TC-017 (lfm2.5:8b), TC-019 (ornith:35b) and TC-021 (lfm2.5-thinking) already pin `think:false` for the same reason.

If you'd rather not have thinking disabled anywhere new, there are two alternatives for TC-022:
1. Raise `num_predict` so the answer fits after the thinking span. It cost 861 thinking characters here, so roughly 500 tokens, and the case gets slower and less deterministic.
2. Keep thinking on and check `thinking` instead of `response`. That diverges from every other case's expect pattern.

I'd keep `think:false`, matching the four existing cases. Say the word and I'll change it.

One workflow-level flow change, outside the testcases: the unload step in `test-models.yml` is now a loop over models found in the testcase YAMLs, instead of 16 hardcoded `curl` lines. Same requests, same `|| true`, just a derived list.

# Open the change request

Target:  — the issue this change closes, if there is one.

**This makes work reviewable. It does not decide whether the work is good.** That judgment
happened already; re-litigating it here means two passes disagreeing with nobody to settle
it. What this checks is mechanical: is the work committed, is it on a branch that is not the
default, does the body link the issue correctly.

**Evidence work never arrives here.** An act performed leaves no diff to review, and its
issue was closed where the act happened. If there is no branch, this is the wrong unit.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh pr create --title "…" --body "…"` | `glab mr create --title "…" --description "…"` |
| target branch | `-B/--base` | `--target-branch` |
| draft | `-d/--draft` | `--draft` |
| body template | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, via `--template` |
| read it back | `gh pr view <N> --json body,url` | `glab mr view <N>` |

**`-d` means different things.** It is `--draft` on `gh` and `--description` on `glab`.
A command copied between them changes meaning without erroring, which is the worst kind of
difference. Write the long flags.

## 1. Is there anything to push

Four checks, and each has a distinct answer when it fails:

- **Committed?** Uncommitted changes mean the work is not finished being recorded. Stop.
- **On a branch that is not the default?** If the commits are on the default branch, go to
  step 1a before anything else.
- **Anything to push at all?** `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` empty means there
  is nothing here. Stop and say so.
- **A change request already open for this branch?** Then this is a push, not an open. Push
  and say the existing one was updated.

Derive the default branch rather than assuming `main`.

## 1a. When the commits are on the default branch

This happens, and it is repairable. Repair it, but never silently.

**Show exactly what would move**, and move nothing else:

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD

**If anything in that list does not belong to this change, stop.** Carrying somebody else's
commits onto this branch is not a call this unit makes.

**Ask before touching history.** On a no, hand back and do not continue to the push, because
pushing from the default branch is the thing this step exists to prevent. On a yes:

    git switch -c <branch-name>
    git branch -f <default> origin/<default>

The first carries the commits onto the new branch. The second rewinds the local default to
what the remote already has. Nothing is discarded and the working tree is never touched,
which is why no hard reset appears here.

**The branch name needs the issue number.** With no issue there is nothing to name it from,
so this is the one case where a missing issue stops the run rather than degrading it.

## 2. Write the body

The issue line depends on what this change request does to its issue:

| This change request | Write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| finishes the issue | the closure keyword and the number | the issue closes on merge, not by hand |
| is one of several for it | `Part of #N` | the issue outlives this change, so a keyword would close it early |
| has no issue | nothing | and the report says this closes nothing |

**A closure keyword fires from anywhere in the body.** The parser reads the keyword and the
number and nothing around them, so a sentence explaining that this change must *not* close
#N will close it. On the middle case, write `Part of #N` and do not mention keywords at all.

Keep the body to what a reviewer needs: what changed, and what they should test. Where the
project ships a change request template, fill that instead of inventing a shape.

## 3. Open it, then read it back

**Push with tracking.** A branch cut locally has no upstream, so the first push sets one:

    git push -u origin <branch>

Without `-u` the push succeeds and later commands that ask "where does this branch go" have
no answer.

**Then create it**, body from a file rather than inline so the closure line survives quoting:

    gh   pr create --title "<title>" --body-file <file>
    glab mr create --title "<title>" --description "$(cat <file>)"

**Then read back what it actually linked**:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,url
    glab mr view <N>

The link is the part that silently goes wrong, and the cost lands later — an issue that
closes early, or one that never closes at all.

Set whatever label marks *under review* in this project, on the issue rather than the change
request. Where the project declares no such label, say so instead of inventing one.

## 4. Stop

A human reviews and tests. This unit does not merge, does not approve, and does not wait.
Say what is open and what the reviewer should exercise, then stop.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Committed, on a non-default branch, with something to push
    - [ ] Commits moved off the default branch if they were on it, after asking
    - [ ] Body written; issue line matches what this change does to the issue
    - [ ] Pushed and opened
    - [ ] Link read back and confirmed
    - [ ] Issue label moved, or its absence stated
    - [ ] Stopped for a human

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, closes it on merge. Reviewer should exercise the upgrade path.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.
    Want the body?

When the commits had to be moved first, that belongs in the first line rather than the
detail, because it is the part a reviewer would not otherwise know happened:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, after moving three commits off main onto issue-27-parser.
    Main is back to origin; nothing was discarded.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

An update to something already open is not a new opening:

    UPDATED — PR #30 already existed for this branch; pushed two more commits to it.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

Refusing is a verdict too:

    NOT OPENED — the tree has uncommitted changes, so this is not finished being recorded.
    Next: commit them, then run this again.

The body, the commit list and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/jack/src/agent-workflows/plugins/agent-workflows/skills/land-pr

# Land the change request

Target:  — the change request to merge.

**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
deleted.** Nothing else about it interests the person who asked. Approvals, protected branch
rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion — all of that is the
repository's route to the outcome, and this unit walks whatever route this repo requires
without asking anyone to know which.

**If the outcome cannot be reached, that is a verdict.** A failure with what blocked it, or
a revise with what must change first. The one thing this must never do is report *merged*
when the code is not in the default branch.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| state | `gh pr view <N> --json mergeStateStatus,headRefOid,headRefName` | `glab mr view <N>` |
| comment | `gh pr comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab mr note <N> -m "…"` |
| merge | `gh pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch` | `glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch` |
| **pin to a SHA** | `--match-head-commit <SHA>` | `--sha <SHA>` |

**The SHA guard is not optional here.** Both platforms can refuse a merge whose head has
moved. A gate that asks about one commit and then merges another has not gated anything, so
pass the confirmed SHA to the merge itself rather than trusting that nothing changed.

## 1. Can it merge

Read the state: conflicts, required checks, required approvals. A change request that cannot
merge does not need a human gate yet — report the blocker and stop, because asking someone
to confirm work that cannot land wastes the one thing this unit spends.

Note the head SHA now. Everything after this is pinned to it.

## 2. The human gate

**Ask outright: has this change been reviewed and tested at `<head SHA>`?**

Three things that do not answer that question, and the reason each is tempting:

- **A green agent pass.** Whatever ran before this was an agent judging its own family of
  work. This gate is a person's judgment on the change as a whole.
- **Being told to run this.** "Merge PR 30" is a request to *reach* this question, never the
  answer to it. Ask, and wait.
- **A confirmation given for a different head.** A person confirmed the diff they were
  shown. If the head has moved since — or moves mid-run — that confirmation does not carry.
  Ask again against the new SHA.

**On no, or on no answer: do not merge.** Stop and report, with the missing confirmation as
the finding. A refused gate owes the reader the same report a merge does.

**On yes, record it before merging**, so the gate leaves a trace someone can find later:

    gh   pr comment <N> --body "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."
    glab mr note    <N> -m     "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."

## 3. Merge

Pass the SHA. Use whatever strategy the project uses, and delete the source branch as part
of the merge rather than afterwards:

    gh   pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch --match-head-commit <SHA>
    glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch --sha <SHA>

**Where the repo requires more than a merge command** — an approval you can request, a check
you can re-run, an auto-merge that lands it when requirements are met — do that. The outcome
is the contract, not the command.

## 4. Establish that it landed

**A command that does not return is not a failure.** It may have succeeded and lost the
connection, timed out while the platform completed it, or genuinely failed. All three look
identical from here, and retrying blind risks acting on a merge that already happened.

**Check the remote, not your working copy:**

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default> -5

The local copy is deliberately stale at this point. Deleting the branch returns you to the
default branch *before* the merge commit has been fetched, so every file the change touched
reads as reverted until the fetch. That intervening state is expected and is not data loss.

**Say which you established.** "Merged, verified at `<sha>` on `origin/<default>`" and
"merge state could not be established" are different reports, and only one of them is a
completion.

## 5. Clean up

**The issue.** Read the body for a closure keyword before assuming it closed:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,closingIssuesReferences
    glab mr view <N>

With a keyword, the merge closed it. Without one, close it by hand and say that is what
happened, because an issue nobody closed reads exactly like an issue nobody finished.

**The labels.** Clear both the pipeline state and any triage state the work carried:

    gh   issue edit <issue> --remove-label <in-progress> --remove-label <triage>
    glab issue update <issue> --unlabel <in-progress> --unlabel <triage>

The triage label is the one nothing upstream removes. Skip this and it strands on closed
work forever, which is how a board fills with things that look actionable and are not.

**The branch and the tree.** The remote branch went with the merge. Remove the local one and
resolve the state step 4 warned about:

    git switch <default>
    git pull
    git branch -d <branch>

`git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch it does not consider merged. That refusal is a
signal worth reading rather than forcing: it means the merge is not visible from here yet,
usually because the pull has not run.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Mergeable — conflicts, checks and approvals read
    - [ ] Head SHA noted; everything after pinned to it
    - [ ] Human asked outright, and answered — not inferred, not assumed
    - [ ] Confirmation recorded on the change request before merging
    - [ ] Merged with the SHA passed to the merge itself
    - [ ] Landing established against the remote default branch
    - [ ] Issue closed, labels cleared, branch gone, back on the default

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    MERGED — PR #30 at a1b2c3d, verified on origin/main. #27 closed, labels cleared,
    branch gone.
    Next: nothing. This has shipped.
    Want the trace?

A refused gate is a verdict and reads the same way:

    NOT MERGED — nobody has confirmed review and test at a1b2c3d.
    Next: someone reviews and tests it, then run this again.

So is an outcome that could not be reached:

    BLOCKED — two required checks are failing, so this cannot land as it stands.
    Next: fix the checks, then run this again.

    UNKNOWN — the merge command did not return and origin/main does not show the commit.
    Next: re-check origin before retrying; a blind retry may act on a merge that landed.

The trace, the checks and the confirmation are prepared and held until asked.

lastPrompt: do we manually run every model test?

content.text:
Yes. Every test workflow in this repo is `workflow_dispatch` only. Nothing runs on push, on a pull request, or on a schedule.

```
.github/workflows/         trigger
──────────────────────     ─────────────────────────────
test-build.yml             workflow_dispatch + workflow_call
test-runtime.yml           workflow_dispatch + workflow_call
test-inference.yml         workflow_dispatch + workflow_call
test-models.yml            workflow_dispatch + workflow_call   ◄ the suite we just trimmed
test-mcp / -context /
  -throughput / -sweep /
  -mlx-smoke              workflow_dispatch
test-pipeline.yml          workflow_dispatch
  └─ build → runtime → inference → models   (chained via workflow_call)
release-docker.yml         release + workflow_dispatch
```

So there are two ways to run the models suite, and both start with you:
1. **`test-models.yml` on its own**, which assumes a testbed is already running the image you want.
2. **`test-pipeline.yml`**, which chains build → runtime → inference → models, each stage gated on the previous one.

The runs bear this out. The last five models runs were all `workflow_dispatch`, and the most recent was 2026-07-28. PR #487 merged without the suite running, because nothing triggers it.

That's a deliberate fit with the hardware: the runner is one self-hosted 4×K80 host, a full models run loads about 180 GB of weights across 19 models, and the slowest ones generate at around 3 tok/s. Running that on every push would keep the box busy for hours and queue behind itself.

Worth considering, if you want less manual work:
- **Dispatch on merges to main only.** A `push: branches: [main]` trigger with `concurrency` set so runs cancel or queue rather than stack up. Still expensive, roughly one full run per merge.
- **A nightly schedule.** `cron` on the models suite, so drift surfaces within a day without blocking any merge.
- **A fast subset on PRs.** The small tags now cover most paths: gemma3:270m, qwen3-vl:2b, ministral-3:3b and deepseek-r1:1.5b total about 6 GB and run in seconds. The runner already accepts an `--id` filter, so a "quick" job is possible without new test code.

Want me to look into any of these? The subset job is the cheapest, and the trim we just landed is what makes it practical.

# `.sessions/` — the reasoning behind the issues

An issue body is a summary, and summarising is where intent shifts. These are the raw
Claude Code session logs that produced them, copied verbatim and linked from the issue.

**The issue binds on scope, the code binds on reality, the log binds on nothing.** It is
background, never specification — read it to find out *why* a decision was made, not to
find out what is true now. An issue must stand on its own; a reader should never *need*
the log, and should almost always *have* it.

## Why this exists

#482 was filed without one. A later agent picking it up could not tell that:

- `qwen3.5:27b` is stale in the unload list because it was **deleted in a disk cleanup**
  earlier in that same session — not because it was never right;
- acceptance criterion 4 names `gemma4:26b`, `gemma3:4b` and the `gpt-oss` variants as
  missing from the models suite, but the session that wrote it meant *"loaded by other
  **suites**"*. They have no `models` testcase; the real gaps are `gemma4:12b`,
  `lfm2.5:8b`, `qwen3.6:27b` and `qwen3.6:35b`;
- the issue exists as a **precondition for the three model ports** (#479, #480, #481),
  which is what decides how it should be fixed.

All three cost a round of questions that the log answers in one read.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Search a Claude Code session log (.jsonl) for credentials, and trim them.

The file-issue workflow copies session logs into .sessions/ and commits them. This
repo is a PUBLIC fork, so a log carrying a live secret publishes it irreversibly.
Run `scan` before committing a log; run `scrub` to write a redacted copy.

Two sources of truth:
  - the built-in regexes below, which recognise secrets by SHAPE and are safe to commit;
  - a local denylist of LITERAL strings, which is not, and so lives outside the repo.

A password like "hunter2" has no shape a regex can catch. Put those literals in the
denylist file (one per line, blank lines and #-comments ignored):

  ~/.claude/scrub-denylist.txt        (override with $SCRUB_DENYLIST_FILE)

Usage:
  scrub-session-log.py scan  <file.jsonl> [...]      exit 1 if anything is found
  scrub-session-log.py scrub <in.jsonl> <out.jsonl>  write a redacted copy
"""

import json
import os
import re
import sys

# Shape-based. Safe to commit — none of these encode a secret.
PATTERNS = [
    ("private-key", r"-----BEGIN (?:[A-Z ]+ )?PRIVATE KEY-----"),
    ("github-token", r"gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}"),
    ("github-pat", r"github_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{30,}"),
    ("anthropic-key", r"sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}"),
    ("openai-key", r"sk-(?:proj-)?[A-Za-z0-9]{32,}"),
    ("aws-access-key", r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}"),
    ("slack-token", r"xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}"),
    ("google-api-key", r"AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}"),
    ("jwt", r"eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}"),
    # [REDACTED-url-inline-cred]host
    ("url-inline-cred", r"[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://[^/\s:@\"\\]+:[^/\s@\"\\]+@"),
    # curl [REDACTED-basic-auth-flag]
    ("basic-auth-flag", r"-u\s+[^\s:\"\\]{1,64}:[^\s\"\\]{4,}"),
    ("auth-header", r"[Aa]uthorization[\"'\s:]+(?:Bearer|Basic|token)\s+[A-Za-z0-9_.=+/-]{8,}"),
    # key = value. ${{ secrets.X }} does not match: '$' is not in the value class.
    ("assigned-secret",
     r"(?i)\b(?:api[_-]?key|apikey|access[_-]?token|auth[_-]?token|secret[_-]?key|password|passwd)\b"
     r"\s*[:=]\s*\\?[\"']?[A-Za-z0-9_.=+/-]{6,}"),
]
COMPILED = [(kind, re.compile(rx)) for kind, rx in PATTERNS]

# Not a credential, but this project's memory forbids publishing the K80 host's address.
PRIVATE_IP = re.compile(r"\b(?:10|127)\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\b"
                        r"|\b192\.168\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\b"
                        r"|\b172\.(?:1[6-9]|2\d|3[01])\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\b")


def load_denylist():
    path = os.environ.get("SCRUB_DENYLIST_FILE",
                          os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/scrub-denylist.txt"))
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return [], path
    literals = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for raw in fh:
            s = raw.strip()
            if s and not s.startswith("#"):
                literals.append(s)
    # longest first, so a substring never redacts ahead of the full secret
    return sorted(set(literals), key=len, reverse=True), path


def mask(s):
    """Show enough to identify a hit, never enough to use it."""
    s = s.strip()
    return (s[:3] + "*" * min(len(s) - 3, 12)) if len(s) > 6 else "*" * len(s)


def find(line, denylist, flag_ips):
    hits = []
    for kind, rx in COMPILED:
        for m in rx.finditer(line):
            hits.append((kind, m.group(0)))
    for lit in denylist:
        if lit in line:
            hits.append(("denylist", lit))
    if flag_ips:
        for m in PRIVATE_IP.finditer(line):
            hits.append(("private-ip", m.group(0)))
    return hits


def redact(line, denylist, flag_ips):
    # Placeholders contain no quotes or backslashes, so JSON stays valid.
    for lit in denylist:
        line = line.replace(lit, "[REDACTED-denylist]")
    for kind, rx in COMPILED:
        line = rx.sub("[REDACTED-%s]" % kind, line)
    if flag_ips:
        line = PRIVATE_IP.sub("[REDACTED-private-ip]", line)
    return line


def main():
    argv = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if a != "--no-ips"]
    flag_ips = "--no-ips" not in sys.argv[1:]
    if len(argv) < 2 or argv[0] not in ("scan", "scrub"):
        print(__doc__.strip())
        return 2

    mode, args = argv[0], argv[1:]
    denylist, denylist_path = load_denylist()
    if not denylist:
        print("WARNING: no denylist at %s — shape-less secrets (plain passwords) "
              "will NOT be caught.\n" % denylist_path, file=sys.stderr)

    if mode == "scan":
        total = 0
        for path in args:
            per_file = {}
            with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
                for n, line in enumerate(fh, 1):
                    for kind, value in find(line, denylist, flag_ips):
                        per_file.setdefault(kind, []).append((n, value))
            if per_file:
                print("%s" % path)
                for kind in sorted(per_file):
                    rows = per_file[kind]
                    lines = ",".join(str(n) for n, _ in rows[:5])
                    more = " +%d" % (len(rows) - 5) if len(rows) > 5 else ""
                    print("  %-18s %3d hit(s)  line %s%s   e.g. %s"
                          % (kind, len(rows), lines, more, mask(rows[0][1])))
                    total += len(rows)
            else:
                print("%s\n  clean" % path)
        print("\n%d finding(s)." % total)
        return 1 if total else 0

    if len(args) != 2:
        print("scrub takes <in.jsonl> <out.jsonl>", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    src, dst = args
    changed = 0
    with open(src, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fin, \
            open(dst, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fout:
        for n, line in enumerate(fin, 1):
            out = redact(line, denylist, flag_ips)
            if out != line:
                changed += 1
            fout.write(out)
            # a redacted log nothing can parse is not a log
            if out.strip():
                try:
                    json.loads(out)
                except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
                    print("ERROR: line %d is not valid JSON after redaction: %s"
                          % (n, e), file=sys.stderr)
                    return 3
    leftover = sum(len(find(l, denylist, flag_ips))
                   for l in open(dst, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"))
    print("%s -> %s: %d line(s) redacted, %d finding(s) remaining"
          % (src, dst, changed, leftover))
    return 1 if leftover else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
